title: Same Behavior, Different Stakes: Rethinking How We Study, Interpret, and Shape LLM Decision-making
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied and deployed as rational agents, models of human behavior, and collaborative decision-making systems. Yet, the same observed behavior can support different conclusions depending on what the model represents and how it is evaluated. Such differences are familiar from studies of human behavior, but the pace of LLM research and reuse of models across settings make them particularly pressing. Inspired by fundamental research contributions at the intersection of AI, game theory and behavioral economics, we propose a taxonomy for making behavioral interpretations of LLMs explicit. We examine how these interpretations should inform research, evaluation, deployment, and the deliberate shaping of LLM behavior. We advocate multidisciplinary awareness to consider alternative interpretations, assess which conclusions remain justified under them, and support exchange between behavioral science and AI. Finally, we discuss limitations of the framework and the scientific and societal risks of interpretive mismatch.

title: From Answers to Interpretations: Rethinking Ambiguity-Induced Aleatoric Uncertainty Estimation in LLMs
abstract: A key challenge in reliable LLM deployment is recognizing when uncertainty reflects irreducible variability in the task rather than limitations in the model's knowledge. In language tasks, a central source of such aleatoric uncertainty is input ambiguity or underspecification, where multiple interpretations remain plausible. Existing decomposition methods estimate aleatoric uncertainty by generating multiple clarifications of the input, querying the model for an answer under each clarification, and comparing the resulting answers. We argue that answers are not necessary for identifying ambiguity: they are often redundant, add avoidable cost, and can mislead through epistemic leakage. We support this claim theoretically, and propose a clarification-only approach that estimates this ambiguity-induced component directly from the space of plausible interpretations, without answers to the clarified inputs. Using ambiguity detection as an operational evaluation across three benchmarks, this direct approach improves AUROC (63.34 vs. 60.85), reduces computational cost by 4–26× in output tokens and 2.2–3.5× in API calls, and yields estimates with substantially lower correlation with epistemic uncertainty. Overall, our results suggest that ambiguity-induced aleatoric uncertainty is better estimated from the interpretation space than from the response space.

title: Motivation in Large Language Models
abstract: Motivation is a central driver of human behavior, shaping decisions, goals, and task performance. As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly aligned with human preferences, we ask whether they exhibit something akin to motivation. We examine whether LLMs "report" varying levels of motivation, how these reports relate to their behavior, and whether external factors can influence them. Our experiments reveal consistent and structured patterns that echo human psychology: self-reported motivation aligns with different behavioral signatures, varies across task types, and can be modulated by external manipulations. These findings demonstrate that motivation is a coherent organizing construct for LLM behavior, systematically linking reports, choices, effort, and performance, and revealing motivational dynamics that resemble those documented in human psychology. This perspective deepens our understanding of model behavior and its connection to human-inspired concepts.

title: Are LLMs Better than Reported? Detecting Label Errors and Mitigating Their Effect on Model Performance
abstract: NLP benchmarks rely on standardized datasets for training and evaluating models and are crucial for advancing the field. Traditionally, expert annotations ensure high-quality labels; however, the cost of expert annotation does not scale well with the growing demand for larger datasets required by modern models. While crowd-sourcing provides a more scalable solution, it often comes at the expense of annotation precision and consistency. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to enhance the annotation process, particularly for detecting label errors in existing datasets. In this work, we consider the recent approach of LLM-as-a-judge, leveraging an ensemble of LLMs to flag potentially mislabeled examples. We conduct a case study on four factual consistency datasets from the TRUE benchmark, spanning diverse NLP tasks, and on SummEval, which uses Likert-scale ratings of summary quality across multiple dimensions. We empirically analyze the labeling quality of existing datasets and compare expert, crowd-sourced, and LLM-based annotations in terms of the agreement, label quality, and efficiency, demonstrating the strengths and limitations of each annotation method. Our findings reveal a substantial number of label errors, which, when corrected, induce a significant upward shift in reported model performance. This suggests that many of the LLMs' so-called mistakes are due to label errors rather than genuine model failures. Additionally, we discuss the implications of mislabeled data and propose methods to mitigate them in training to improve performance.

title: Transition Function Prediction in AI Planning Using LLMs
venue: AAAI 2025 Workshop on Language Models for Planning (LM4Plan)
abstract: Classical AI planning requires an explicit transition function describing how actions change the environment. Constructing these transition models is often labor-intensive and requires domain expertise. In this work, we investigate whether large language models can predict transition functions directly from natural language descriptions of planning domains. We evaluate LLMs on their ability to infer action effects and state transitions across a range of planning tasks. Our results show that LLMs can often generate plausible transition models, suggesting a promising direction for integrating language models into planning pipelines. At the same time, we identify systematic limitations and discuss challenges in reliability and correctness when using LLM-generated transition functions for downstream planning tasks.

title: Decongestion by Representation: Learning to Improve Economic Welfare in Marketplaces
abstract: Many marketplaces suffer from congestion: when too many users select the same resources, overall welfare decreases. In this work, we introduce Decongestion by Representation, a learning framework that improves economic welfare by shaping the representation used by decision-making agents. Rather than modifying incentives or imposing coordination mechanisms, the approach modifies the information representation provided to agents so that individually rational decisions lead to better collective outcomes. Experiments in simulated marketplace environments demonstrate that the learned representations significantly reduce congestion and increase overall welfare while preserving agents' ability to optimize their own objectives.
